readerContract.humanQuestion: Did an AI brain implant let people communicate more naturally, and what does the research actually show?
readerContract.promisedPayoff: Understand what the implant decoded, who tested it, and why this is a research step rather than an available treatment.
readerContract.priorKnowledge: A reader may see an avatar and assume a brain implant can now restore conversation.
readerContract.centralMentalModel: The implant records brain signals; separately trained decoders turn a limited set of attempted phrases and gestures into on-screen text and avatar movement. That is a tested proof of concept, not normal conversation on demand.
readerContract.dailyLifeConnection: When a health-AI headline promises communication restored, a reader can ask who used it, what signals were decoded, and whether the system was tested beyond a lab demonstration.
readerContract.surfaceJob: A short dated research-news explanation of a peer-reviewed brain-computer-interface study.
readerContract.desiredFeeling: I can separate a striking demonstration from an available medical option without dismissing why it matters.

draftArchitecture.plainAnswer: Researchers showed that one implanted ECoG array can decode attempted speech and upper-body gestures at the same time in a limited research demonstration; it is not an available treatment.
causalSequence: An ECoG array records brain activity from the motor cortex of people with severe paralysis.
Two decoders trained on both isolated and simultaneous attempts convert a limited trained set of signals into text and avatar gestures.
Training only on separate attempts did not fully carry over to combined attempts, so the study demonstrates a technical step and a remaining challenge.
draftArchitecture.workedCase: A participant attempts a trained phrase and gesture; the system displays the decoded text and animates the paired avatar gesture.
draftArchitecture.transferCase: For a later medical-AI headline, ask whether people used the system outside a prepared task and whether it changed patient care.
draftArchitecture.usefulAction: Treat this as a research result and check participant count, training task, hardware and clinical availability before sharing it as a treatment breakthrough.
draftArchitecture.formatSpecificStructure: The Story; LAiDIES Read; What This Means for You; Cocktail Party; Class Notes.
draftArchitecture.antiTemplateDecision: No speculation about approval, timelines, independence or individual outcomes; no promise that an implant reads free-form thoughts.

explanationArc.adaptation: A compact research-news explanation, not a clinical guide.

discoveryChecks.question: Did the implant restore free-form conversation?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. The study decoded a restricted trained set of attempted phrases and gestures in a laboratory task.

discoveryChecks.question: Did all three participants control the simultaneous speech-and-gesture avatar?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. Three participants contributed movement-decoding evidence; the simultaneous avatar demonstration involved two participants.

discoveryChecks.question: Is this an available treatment or proof of better health outcomes?
discoveryChecks.answer: No. It is a wired proof-of-concept system; larger cohorts, broader repertoires and further testing remain necessary.

representativeProofPlan.highestRisk: Turning a limited avatar demonstration into a claim that the device restores ordinary conversation or is clinically available.
representativeProofPlan.plannedProof: Every consequential claim is limited to the three-participant paper and NIH release; the draft must name the limited trained expressions, wired setup and further-testing need.
representativeProofPlan.acceptanceOutcome: A reader can say what the implant decoded in the study and why that is not a treatment claim.
